q: This first governing document of the United States, ratified in 1781, created a weak national government with no power to tax and no executive. Shays' Rebellion exposed its weakness. For 10 points, name this document replaced by the Constitution.

This Greek philosopher's Politics classified governments by how many rule and whether they rule for the common good, naming monarchy, aristocracy and polity. He declared that "man is by nature a political animal." For 10 points, name this tutor of Alexander the Great.

This American anthropologist, often called the father of American anthropology, taught at Columbia University and promoted cultural relativism. He rejected racial theories and mentored Margaret Mead and Ruth Benedict. For 10 points, name this German-born scholar.

This anthropologist's 1928 book Coming of Age in Samoa argued that adolescence in Samoa was less stressful than in America. She studied under Franz Boas. For 10 points, name this author, who later wrote Sex and Temperament.

This Polish-born anthropologist did fieldwork on the Trobriand Islands and wrote Argonauts of the Western Pacific. He pioneered the method of participant observation. For 10 points, name this founder of functionalism in anthropology.

In the Trobriand Islands, Malinowski described this ceremonial exchange of shell necklaces and armbands traveling in opposite directions between islands. For 10 points, name this system of exchange, whose name rhymes with "ring" at the end.

This French anthropologist founded structuralism in anthropology with works such as The Elementary Structures of Kinship and Tristes Tropiques. He analyzed myths through binary oppositions like raw and cooked. For 10 points, name this scholar, first name Claude.

This American anthropologist, author of The Interpretation of Cultures, advocated "thick description" in studying culture. He studied religion in Bali and Java. For 10 points, name this scholar, first name Clifford.

This anthropologist's 1934 book Patterns of Culture compared the Zuni, Dobu and Kwakiutl, arguing that each culture has a distinctive personality. She also wrote The Chrysanthemum and the Sword. For 10 points, name this student of Franz Boas.

This principle, championed by Franz Boas, holds that a person's beliefs and activities should be understood in terms of their own culture, not judged by others' standards. For 10 points, name this concept contrasting with ethnocentrism.
Among peoples of the Pacific Northwest Coast, like the Kwakiutl, this ceremonial feast involves giving away or destroying wealth to gain prestige. For 10 points, name this gift-giving ceremony.

Arnold van Gennep identified three stages in this kind of ceremony: separation, transition and incorporation. Examples include baptisms, weddings and graduations. For 10 points, name this type of ritual that marks a change in social status.

Victor Turner expanded on van Gennep's work by developing this concept, from the Latin for "threshold," describing the in-between stage of a ritual in which participants are neither one status nor the next. For 10 points, name this term.

This word, from a Polynesian language, names something forbidden by social or religious custom. Sigmund Freud wrote about its "totem" companion. For 10 points, name this word for a prohibition, such as the incest one.
In 1974, Donald Johanson found a skeleton in Ethiopia of this 3.2-million-year-old hominin, named after a Beatles song. For 10 points, give this nickname of the Australopithecus afarensis fossil.

This East African gorge in Tanzania was the site of Louis and Mary Leakey's discoveries of early hominins, including Homo habilis. For 10 points, name this gorge, whose name sounds like a type of bird.

This extinct relative of modern humans lived in Europe and western Asia, made Mousterian tools, and buried its dead. Its name comes from a German valley. For 10 points, name this species, Homo neanderthalensis.
This hominin species, whose name means "upright man," used fire and made Acheulean hand axes. Its fossils include Java Man and Peking Man. For 10 points, name this species, Homo erectus.
This revolution, around 10,000 years ago, saw humans shift from hunting and gathering to farming and settling in villages. For 10 points, name this period, named for the "new stone" age.

This radiometric technique, developed by Willard Libby, measures the decay of an unstable isotope in organic remains to date objects up to about fifty thousand years old. For 10 points, name this dating method.

This English anthropologist defined culture in 1871 as "that complex whole which includes knowledge, belief, art, morals, law, custom" and other capabilities in his book Primitive Culture. For 10 points, name this pioneering scholar, first name Edward Burnett.

This American anthropologist wrote Ancient Society and studied the Iroquois, devising an evolutionary scheme of savagery, barbarism and civilization. He also wrote on kinship systems. For 10 points, name this scholar, first name Lewis Henry.

This anthropologist's study of the Yanomami of the Amazon, titled Yanomamo: The Fierce People, became controversial. He studied violence and warfare. For 10 points, name this American anthropologist, first name Napoleon.

This term names the transmission of customs, ideas or technologies from one culture to another, as when papermaking spread from China along the Silk Road to the Islamic world and Europe. Anthropologists contrast it with independent invention. For 10 points, name this spread of cultural traits between societies.

In anthropology, this term names the system of social relationships based on blood, marriage and adoption. Lewis Henry Morgan was a pioneer in its study. For 10 points, name this concept of family ties.

This hoax of 1912, in which a skull was supposedly the "missing link," was exposed in 1953 as a human cranium combined with an orangutan jaw. For 10 points, name this fraud, named for a town in Sussex.

This Turkish archaeological site, dating to about 9500 BCE, consists of massive carved T-shaped pillars arranged in circles, apparently built by hunter-gatherers before farming. For 10 points, name this site near Sanliurfa.

This African American anthropologist wrote Mules and Men and studied folklore in Florida and Haiti. She is better known for the novel Their Eyes Were Watching God. For 10 points, name this Harlem Renaissance writer.

This South African anatomist described the Taung Child in 1925 and proposed that Africa, not Asia, was the cradle of humankind. For 10 points, name this scientist who named Australopithecus africanus.

This term names an animal species or plant used as an emblem of a clan, believed to be an ancestor or protector. Carved poles from the Pacific Northwest depict them. For 10 points, name this kind of emblem.
These societies, like the !Kung of the Kalahari, rely on foraging wild plants and hunting animals, and are typically nomadic and egalitarian. For 10 points, name this type of society.

q: In 1978, this British-born archaeologist discovered preserved hominin footprints about 3.6 million years old in volcanic ash at Laetoli in Tanzania. She was the wife of Louis Leakey. For 10 points, name this scientist who also found the skull of Proconsul.

This American linguist's 1957 book Syntactic Structures introduced transformational grammar. He proposed that humans have an innate "universal grammar" and wrote the sentence "Colorless green ideas sleep furiously." For 10 points, name this MIT professor.

This term names the smallest unit of sound in a language that can distinguish one word from another, such as the difference between "bat" and "pat." For 10 points, name this unit of sound, a basic concept in phonology.
This term names the smallest meaningful unit in a language. The word "unhappiness" contains three of them: un-, happy and -ness. For 10 points, name these units, studied in morphology.

This branch of linguistics studies the rules by which words are combined into phrases and sentences. Word order, such as subject-verb-object, is one of its main concerns. For 10 points, name this field.

This Swiss linguist's posthumous Course in General Linguistics distinguished between langue and parole and described the sign as made of signifier and signified. For 10 points, name this founder of structural linguistics, first name Ferdinand.

This hypothesis, named for two American linguists, claims that the structure of a language shapes how its speakers perceive the world. It is also called linguistic relativity. For 10 points, name this idea associated with Edward Sapir and Benjamin Lee Whorf.

This type of simplified contact language arises between groups with no common language, usually for trade, and has no native speakers. When children grow up speaking one, it becomes a creole. For 10 points, name this kind of language.
A language of this type develops when a pidgin becomes the native language of a community. Haitian and Jamaican Patois are examples. For 10 points, name this kind of fully developed language.

This hypothetical ancestor of English, Latin, Greek, Sanskrit and many other languages was reconstructed by comparing cognates. William Jones noted similarities among Sanskrit, Greek and Latin in 1786. For 10 points, name this reconstructed language, abbreviated PIE.

This sound law, named for a German folklorist and linguist who also co-edited fairy tales, describes how Indo-European stops shifted in Germanic languages, as in Latin pater becoming English father. For 10 points, name this law named for Jacob.

This system, abbreviated IPA, uses a standard set of symbols for the sounds of all spoken languages. Linguists and language learners use it in dictionaries and textbooks to write pronunciations unambiguously. For 10 points, name this alphabet used in dictionaries to show pronunciation.

This unstressed vowel, written with an upside-down e, is the most common vowel sound in English, as in the first syllable of "about." It occurs in the final syllable of "sofa" and the first syllable of "banana." Reduced vowels in unstressed syllables often take this sound. For 10 points, name this mid-central vowel.

This type of vowel sound consists of two vowels in a single syllable, as in "boy," "out" and "ride." English words like "coin" and "cow" contain this. A single vowel sound, by contrast, is called a monophthong. For 10 points, name this gliding vowel, from Greek for "two sounds."
This word names a variety of a language spoken in a region or by a social group, with its own vocabulary and grammar, such as Southern American English. For 10 points, name this term.

This practice involves alternating between two languages or varieties in a single conversation or even a sentence. Bilingual speakers of Spanish and English often do it. For 10 points, name this term.
This French scholar deciphered Egyptian hieroglyphs in 1822 using the Rosetta Stone, which carries the same text in three scripts. For 10 points, name this man, first name Jean-Francois.

This constructed language was created in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof as a neutral international auxiliary language. Zamenhof was a Polish ophthalmologist who published it under a pen name meaning "Doctor Hopeful." It has no irregular verbs. For 10 points, name this language whose name means "one who hopes."

This language of northern Spain and southwestern France is a language isolate, unrelated to any other known language. It is spoken in a region whose people call themselves Euskaldunak. For 10 points, name this language.

This Korean alphabet was created by King Sejong the Great in the fifteenth century so that ordinary people could read and write. Its letters are arranged into syllable blocks. For 10 points, name this script.
This Cherokee silversmith invented a syllabary in the 1820s that allowed his people to become literate within a few years. For 10 points, name this man, whose name is also borne by giant trees.

This area in the left frontal lobe is involved in producing speech. Damage to it causes a type of aphasia in which patients understand language but speak haltingly. For 10 points, name this area named for a French physician.
This English architect and cryptographer deciphered Linear B in 1952, showing it recorded an early form of Greek. He worked with John Chadwick. For 10 points, name this man, first name Michael.

This feature of Mandarin Chinese and Vietnamese is the use of pitch patterns on syllables to distinguish word meaning. The syllable "ma" can mean mother or horse depending on it. For 10 points, name this feature, such as in a "tonal language."

Turkish and Japanese are examples of this type of language, in which words are built by stringing together many affixes, each with one meaning. For 10 points, name this morphological type whose name comes from the Latin for "glue together."

A word of this type is borrowed from one language into another, such as "tsunami" from Japanese or "pajamas" from Hindi. English has many from French, such as "restaurant," after the Norman Conquest. Linguists study how they are adapted to the sounds of the borrowing language. For 10 points, name this kind of word.

In this branch of linguistics, scholars study how context contributes to meaning, such as how "Can you pass the salt?" is a request rather than a question about ability. For 10 points, name this field, which comes after semantics in the list.

This branch of linguistics studies the origins and historical development of words. The word "salary" comes from the Latin word for salt in it. For 10 points, name this field, which is not entomology.

This large group of more than five hundred languages includes Swahili, Zulu and Shona and is spoken across much of central and southern Africa. The word "ubuntu" belongs to it, and its own name means "people." For 10 points, name this language group.

This California girl, found in 1970 after being locked in a room for her entire childhood, was studied by linguists to test the critical period hypothesis for language acquisition. For 10 points, give the pseudonym used for this girl.

These consonant sounds, such as p, t and k, are made by completely blocking the airflow in the vocal tract and then releasing it. English "b" and "d" are voiced examples. For 10 points, name this class of consonants, also called plosives.

q: This painting hangs in the Louvre behind protective glass. It was painted with a hazy technique called sfumato, and its sitter is traditionally identified as Lisa Gherardini. The sitter's enigmatic smile has fascinated viewers for centuries. For 10 points, name this portrait by Leonardo da Vinci.

This artist painted The Starry Night while staying at an asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. He applied paint in thick, swirling strokes and painted several canvases of sunflowers. He famously cut off part of his own ear. For 10 points, name this Dutch Post-Impressionist.

This artist's Blue Period came after the suicide of his friend Carlos Casagemas. He painted a huge black-and-white mural about the bombing of a Basque town and the Spanish Civil War. He also painted Les Demoiselles d'Avignon. For 10 points, name this Spanish painter who worked in Paris.

This artist painted a ceiling in the Vatican with scenes from the Book of Genesis, including The Creation of Adam. He lay on scaffolding for years to finish it, and also carved the Pietà. For 10 points, name this Italian artist of the Sistine Chapel.

This painter's Persistence of Memory shows soft melting watches in a barren landscape. He was known for his upturned waxed mustache and his dreamlike imagery. He was born in Figueres, in Catalonia. For 10 points, name this Spanish painter.

This artist made silkscreen prints of Campbell's Soup cans and of Marilyn Monroe. He ran a New York studio called the Factory. He said everyone would be famous for fifteen minutes. For 10 points, name this leading figure of pop art.

This painter is known for her many self-portraits, such as The Two Fridas, which often show her thick eyebrows. She lived in a blue house in Coyoacán in Mexico City. She was married to a famous muralist. For 10 points, name this Mexican painter.

This artist dripped and poured paint onto huge canvases laid on the floor. His method was called action painting, and his works include Lavender Mist and Autumn Rhythm. He worked in Springs, New York. For 10 points, name this American Abstract Expressionist.

This art movement is named after a hazy Claude Monet seascape of a sunrise. Its painters, including Renoir and Degas, captured fleeting effects of light, often painting outdoors. They used short, visible brushstrokes. For 10 points, name this nineteenth-century French art movement.

This Dutch Golden Age painter made dozens of self-portraits throughout his life. His group portrait of a militia company, The Night Watch, is in the Rijksmuseum. He was a master of dramatic light and shadow. For 10 points, name this artist of The Anatomy Lesson of Dr. Tulp.

This painter lived in Delft and made small, quiet interior scenes lit by a window, such as The Milkmaid. He also painted a portrait of a girl wearing a blue and yellow turban. For 10 points, name this Dutch artist of Girl with a Pearl Earring.

This Florentine painter showed a nude goddess standing on a giant scallop shell in a painting for the Medici family. He also painted Primavera. For 10 points, name this Italian Renaissance artist of The Birth of Venus.

This painter's most famous work shows a stern farmer holding a pitchfork beside a woman in front of a white house with a pointed window. The models were his dentist and his sister. For 10 points, name this Iowa artist of American Gothic.

This artist painted close-up views of flowers, as well as bleached animal skulls against the desert sky. She spent her later years in New Mexico, near Ghost Ranch. For 10 points, name this American painter of Black Iris.

This mural was painted on a refectory wall of the Convent of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan. It shows twelve men reacting as their leader announces that one of them will betray him. For 10 points, name this Leonardo da Vinci painting of Jesus and his apostles.

This French artist led the Fauves, whose paintings use bright, wild colors. Late in life, he made cut-paper collages such as The Snail. His works include The Dance and The Red Studio. For 10 points, name this French painter.

This American painter depicted lonely figures in a late-night diner in a work titled Nighthawks. He also painted Early Sunday Morning and House by the Railroad. His paintings capture urban isolation. For 10 points, name this realist painter.

This statue stands over seventeen feet tall in the Galleria dell'Accademia in Florence. It was carved from a single block of marble by Michelangelo and shows a young shepherd before a battle with a giant. For 10 points, name this statue of a biblical hero.
This French sculptor made a bronze of a nude man sitting with his chin on his fist, The Thinker. He also carved The Kiss and made the Gates of Hell. For 10 points, name this sculptor.

Georges Seurat's A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte is a famous example of this technique. Paul Signac also used it, placing small dots of pure color side by side so they blend in the viewer's eye. For 10 points, name this painting technique that uses tiny dots.

This American artist moved to Paris, where she exhibited with Edgar Degas and the Impressionists. She painted tender scenes of mothers and children, such as The Child's Bath. For 10 points, name this woman who painted The Boating Party.

This American illustrator painted many covers for The Saturday Evening Post. His series Four Freedoms includes Freedom from Want, a Thanksgiving scene. His Rosie the Riveter was a cover from 1943. For 10 points, name this artist.

This Japanese artist's woodblock print shows a huge curling wave about to swamp fishing boats, with a small Mount Fuji in the distance. It is part of his series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji. For 10 points, name this ukiyo-e artist of The Great Wave off Kanagawa.

This Mexican artist painted the Detroit Industry murals. His mural for Rockefeller Center was destroyed after he included a portrait of Lenin. He painted giant murals at the National Palace in Mexico City. For 10 points, name this muralist.

This word means "rebirth" in French. This period began in Florence in the fourteenth century and produced artists like Raphael and Leonardo. It revived interest in the art of ancient Greece and Rome. For 10 points, give this term for the era that followed the Middle Ages in Europe.

Painters traditionally say that these colors cannot be made by mixing other colors. Mixing two of them produces colors like orange and green. They are red, yellow, and blue. For 10 points, name this set of three basic colors.

Georges Braque and the painter of Guernica worked together on this style, which has analytic and synthetic phases. Its paintings break objects into geometric shapes and show them from several viewpoints at once. For 10 points, name this twentieth-century art movement.

This painting medium uses pigments mixed with water, and the paint is applied to paper in thin, transparent layers. The paper shows through, and white areas are usually left unpainted. For 10 points, name this medium used by Winslow Homer and John Singer Sargent.

The Sistine Chapel ceiling was made using this method, in which artists paint on wet plaster so that the pigment becomes part of the wall. Its name is Italian for "fresh." For 10 points, name this mural technique.

This Italian polymath drew the Vitruvian Man and filled notebooks with designs for flying machines. He painted The Virgin of the Rocks and was born in the town of Vinci. His notebooks were written in mirror script. For 10 points, name this Renaissance artist of the Mona Lisa.

q: This composer kept writing music after going deaf. He wrote nine symphonies, including one whose last movement sets Schiller's Ode to Joy. He also wrote the Moonlight Sonata. For 10 points, name this German composer of the Fifth Symphony.

This composer was a child prodigy who toured Europe with his sister Nannerl. He lived in Vienna and wrote The Marriage of Figaro and The Magic Flute. He wrote the Requiem, which was left unfinished. For 10 points, name this Austrian composer.

This composer worked as a church musician in Leipzig. He wrote six Brandenburg Concertos and The Well-Tempered Clavier. He was a master of the fugue and had many musical children. For 10 points, name this German Baroque composer.

This instrument has four strings tuned to G, D, A, and E and is played with a horsehair bow. It is the highest-pitched string instrument in the orchestra's string section. Antonio Stradivari made famous ones in Cremona. For 10 points, name this instrument.

This instrument was invented by Bartolomeo Cristofori in Italy around 1700. Pressing a key makes a felt hammer strike a string. A standard one has 88 keys. For 10 points, name this keyboard instrument.

This Italian term, abbreviated with the letter f in sheet music, tells the performer to play loudly. Its opposite is piano, and its stronger version is fortissimo. Composers write these dynamic markings below the staff. For 10 points, give this musical dynamic marking.
This Russian composer wrote the ballets Swan Lake and The Nutcracker. His 1812 Overture ends with cannon fire. His Sixth Symphony is called the Pathétique. For 10 points, name this Romantic composer.

This Baroque composer wrote four violin concertos named for the seasons. Born in Venice, he worked at a school for orphaned girls, the Ospedale della Pietà, and was a priest with red hair. He wrote hundreds of concertos and the oratorio Juditha triumphans. For 10 points, name this Baroque composer of The Four Seasons.

This band from Liverpool included John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison, and Ringo Starr. Its albums include Abbey Road and Sergeant Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band. For 10 points, name this British rock band of "Hey Jude."

This New Orleans trumpeter was nicknamed Satchmo. He sang with a gravelly voice on "What a Wonderful World" and led groups called the Hot Five and the Hot Seven. For 10 points, name this jazz musician.

This person stands on a podium in front of an orchestra and uses a baton to keep time. This person also controls the tempo and shapes the interpretation of the music. For 10 points, name this leader of an orchestra or choir.
This art form is Italian for "work," and combines singing, an orchestra, costumes, and acting on stage. La Traviata and Carmen are examples. For 10 points, name this form of musical drama.
This German composer wrote Hungarian Dances and a famous lullaby beginning "Guten Abend, gut' Nacht." He wrote four symphonies and a German Requiem. For 10 points, name this Romantic composer.

This American composer wrote Rhapsody in Blue and the opera Porgy and Bess. His orchestral work An American in Paris includes taxi horns. His brother Ira wrote lyrics. For 10 points, name this composer.

This composer died at age thirty-one after writing hundreds of songs. His Unfinished Symphony has only two completed movements. He also set Goethe's poem Erlkönig to music. For 10 points, name this Viennese composer of Winterreise.

This Polish composer wrote mostly for solo piano, including nocturnes, waltzes, polonaises, and mazurkas. He moved to Paris and had a relationship with the writer George Sand. For 10 points, name this Romantic pianist.

This is the largest ensemble form in classical music, usually in four movements and played by a full orchestra. Haydn wrote more than one hundred of them. For 10 points, give this term for a long orchestral work.

This American genre grew out of New Orleans and relies on improvisation and syncopated rhythms. Swing, bebop, and Dixieland are types. For 10 points, name this genre played by Duke Ellington and Miles Davis.

This composer wrote the ballets Petrushka and The Firebird for Sergei Diaghilev's Ballets Russes. He was born in Russia but later became an American citizen. His pulsing, dissonant 1913 ballet about a pagan sacrifice caused a scandal in Paris. For 10 points, name this Russian-born composer.

This American composer wrote the ballet Appalachian Spring and Fanfare for the Common Man. His music uses open harmonies and folk tunes. He also wrote the ballet Rodeo. For 10 points, name this composer.
This French composer wrote Clair de lune and La mer. He also wrote Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun. His music is associated with Impressionism. For 10 points, name this composer.
This woodwind instrument has no reed. The player blows across a hole near one end, and the instrument is held sideways. The piccolo is a smaller relative. For 10 points, name this instrument.

This Austrian composer, nicknamed "Papa," wrote the Surprise Symphony and the Farewell Symphony. He spent years working for the Esterházy family and taught Beethoven. For 10 points, name this composer.
This oratorio by George Frideric Handel premiered in Dublin in 1742. Audiences traditionally stand during its Hallelujah chorus. For 10 points, name this oratorio about the life of Christ.

This singer was born in Tupelo, Mississippi, and rose to fame at Sun Records in Memphis. Known as the King of Rock and Roll, he recorded "Hound Dog" and "Jailhouse Rock" and lived at Graceland. For 10 points, name this American singer.

At the beginning of a line of sheet music, this symbol shows which pitches the lines and spaces stand for. The G one swirls around the second line of the staff. For 10 points, name this symbol, such as treble or bass.
Timpani, snare drums, cymbals, and xylophones belong to this family of instruments. They are played by striking, shaking, or scraping. For 10 points, name this section of the orchestra.

This interval spans eight diatonic scale degrees, such as from one C to the next C. The two notes sound very similar because their frequencies are in a ratio of two to one. For 10 points, name this interval.

This German composer built his own opera house in Bayreuth, the Festspielhaus, to stage his works. He wrote The Ring of the Nibelung, which includes The Valkyrie. He used leitmotifs. For 10 points, name this composer.

This brass instrument has three valves and a bright, piercing tone. Louis Armstrong and Miles Davis played it, and it often plays fanfares in orchestras and marching bands. For 10 points, name this high brass instrument.

q: This film series begins with a scrolling yellow text crawl and a ship chased by a huge star destroyer. Its characters include Luke Skywalker, Princess Leia, and Han Solo. Fans say "May the Force be with you." For 10 points, name this space opera created by George Lucas.

This 1939 film begins in black and white in Kansas, then turns to color when the heroine arrives in a magical land. Judy Garland sang "Over the Rainbow" in it. The heroine follows a yellow brick road with a Scarecrow, a Tin Man, and a Cowardly Lion. For 10 points, name this film based on a book by L. Frank Baum.

This man created Mickey Mouse and produced the first full-length cel-animated feature, Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs. He opened a California theme park in 1955. His studio also produced Cinderella and Bambi. For 10 points, name this American animator.

This director made a movie about a great white shark terrorizing Amity Island. He also directed E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial, Jurassic Park, and Schindler's List. He co-founded DreamWorks. For 10 points, name this American filmmaker.

This 1997 film shows a romance between Jack and Rose aboard an ocean liner that strikes an iceberg. It features the song "My Heart Will Go On" sung by Celine Dion. Its stars are Leonardo DiCaprio and Kate Winslet. For 10 points, name this James Cameron film.

This British-born director is called the "Master of Suspense." He made Psycho, with its famous shower scene, and Vertigo. He appeared in brief cameos in most of his films. For 10 points, name this director of Rear Window and The Birds.

This 1995 film was the first feature-length movie made entirely with computer animation. It follows a cowboy doll who is jealous when a space ranger action figure becomes his owner Andy's favorite toy. For 10 points, name this Pixar film starring Woody and Buzz Lightyear.

This 1994 Disney film follows a lion cub who flees after his father Mufasa is killed by his uncle Scar. Its songs by Elton John include "Circle of Life," and it features the phrase "Hakuna Matata." For 10 points, name this animated film about Simba.

Orson Welles directed and starred in this 1941 film, which many critics rank among the best ever made. It begins with a dying newspaper magnate whispering the word "Rosebud." The title character is loosely based on William Randolph Hearst. For 10 points, name this film.

This British-born comic actor played a mustached character called the Tramp. He directed and starred in silent films such as The Kid and Modern Times. He cofounded United Artists. For 10 points, name this star of The Gold Rush.

This animated sitcom set in the town of Springfield was created by Matt Groening. Its title family includes Homer, Marge, Bart, Lisa, and Maggie. It premiered as a series on Fox in 1989. For 10 points, name this long-running show.

In this 1942 film, Humphrey Bogart plays Rick Blaine, who runs a nightclub in Morocco. Ingrid Bergman plays Ilsa, and the film includes the line "Here's looking at you, kid." The song "As Time Goes By" is featured. For 10 points, name this classic wartime romance.

This 1939 epic stars Vivien Leigh as Scarlett O'Hara and Clark Gable as Rhett Butler. It is set in Georgia during the Civil War and Reconstruction, and it ends with the line "Frankly, my dear, I don't give a damn." For 10 points, name this film based on Margaret Mitchell's novel.

This New Zealand director filmed a trilogy of films based on Tolkien's books about a ring that must be destroyed. The trilogy's final film won eleven Academy Awards in 2004. He later directed a trilogy of films based on The Hobbit. For 10 points, name this director.

This Japanese director made Rashomon, which tells one crime from conflicting viewpoints. His film Seven Samurai inspired the American Western The Magnificent Seven. He often worked with the actor Toshiro Mifune. For 10 points, name this filmmaker of Ran and Yojimbo.

This Japanese director cofounded Studio Ghibli. His films include My Neighbor Totoro, Princess Mononoke, and Spirited Away, which won the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature. For 10 points, name this animator.

These annual honors are given by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. A golden statuette awarded to winners has a nickname that is often used for the prizes themselves. For 10 points, name these awards for film, which include Best Picture.

This long-running children's television show on PBS takes place on a city street and features Big Bird, Elmo, Oscar the Grouch, and Cookie Monster. It premiered in 1969. For 10 points, name this show.

This Soviet director made Battleship Potemkin, which includes a famous massacre on the Odessa Steps. He developed theories about montage, in which editing creates meaning through juxtaposition. For 10 points, name this director of Strike and October.

This director made 2001: A Space Odyssey, with its sentient computer HAL 9000. He also directed Dr. Strangelove, The Shining, and A Clockwork Orange. He was known for perfectionism and long shoots. For 10 points, name this American-born British filmmaker.

Before filming a movie, directors often use this tool, which is a series of drawings that show each shot in order, like a comic strip. Animators also create it to plan scenes. For 10 points, name this planning tool.

In movies, these three letters stand for a technology that makes digital images and creatures, such as the dinosaurs of Jurassic Park and the Na'vi of Avatar. For 10 points, give this abbreviation for computer-generated imagery.

Released in 1927, this film starring Al Jolson is generally credited as the first feature-length movie with synchronized dialogue. It features songs and spoken lines, and it ended the era of silent films. For 10 points, name this film about a cantor's son who defies his father to perform popular music.

This silent film star was nicknamed "the Great Stone Face" because he almost never smiled. He did his own dangerous stunts in films such as The General and Sherlock Jr. For 10 points, name this American comedian.

In 1895, these two French brothers held a public screening of short films in a Paris cafe using their cinématographe. Auguste and Louis ran a photographic plate business in Lyon. For 10 points, name these early filmmakers whose surname means "light" in French.

This cartoon rabbit from Looney Tunes chews a carrot and asks "What's up, Doc?" He often outsmarts the hunter Elmer Fudd and the black duck Daffy, and he first appeared in the 1940 short A Wild Hare. For 10 points, name this Warner Bros. character.

In this 1950s sitcom, a redheaded woman gets into schemes while her husband Ricky Ricardo leads a band. Its title character was played by Lucille Ball. It was one of the first shows to be filmed before a live audience. For 10 points, name this show.
This puppeteer created Kermit the Frog and the other Muppets. He worked on Sesame Street and also directed The Dark Crystal. For 10 points, name this American creator of Fozzie Bear and Miss Piggy.

In film production, this person adds sounds like footsteps and breaking glass in a studio, matching them to actions on screen. For 10 points, give this job title, named for the sound-effects pioneer Jack.

This 1927 German silent science-fiction film directed by Fritz Lang is set in a city of towers where workers toil underground. It features a robot double of a woman named Maria. For 10 points, name this film.

q: This wrought-iron lattice tower was built for the 1889 World's Fair. It was designed by the firm of Gustave Eiffel, and many Parisians first protested it. It stands on the Champ de Mars. For 10 points, name this landmark of Paris.

This monument was built for the pharaoh Khufu on the west bank of the Nile. It was made from millions of limestone blocks and is the largest of the pyramids at its site. For 10 points, name this ancient Egyptian tomb near Cairo.

This elliptical amphitheater in Rome was built under the Flavian emperors and could seat tens of thousands. It hosted gladiator fights and had underground tunnels called the hypogeum. For 10 points, name this ruined arena.

This marble temple stands on the Acropolis in Athens and was dedicated to the goddess Athena. It was built in the fifth century BC in the Doric style and designed by Ictinus and Callicrates. For 10 points, name this ancient Greek temple.

This white marble mausoleum in Agra, India, was built by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan. He built it for his wife Mumtaz Mahal. It has four minarets and a large central dome. For 10 points, name this building.

This long fortification stretches across northern China. Built and rebuilt over many dynasties, it was meant to protect against nomadic invaders. Its Ming dynasty sections are best known. For 10 points, name this structure.

This American architect designed Fallingwater, a house built over a waterfall in Pennsylvania. He developed the Prairie School and designed the spiraling Guggenheim Museum in New York City. For 10 points, name this architect who founded Taliesin.

This style developed in medieval France and features pointed arches, ribbed vaults, and large stained-glass windows. Cathedrals built in it use flying buttresses to support high walls. For 10 points, name this architectural style of Chartres and Reims.

This building type has a steel frame that supports its weight, allowing great height. The invention of the safety elevator by Elisha Otis helped make it practical. Chicago and New York pioneered it. For 10 points, name this type of very tall building.
